common_name: Diane Witch Hazel (Red-Flowered Winter Witch Hazel)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; witch hazel flower buds need real winter chill to open well, so bloom is most reliable in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 and can be sparse in mild winters.

directions: Diane is the most widely grown red-flowered witch hazel, producing clusters of narrow, spidery, ribbon-petaled flowers in a deep coppery red that opens in late winter while the shrub is still bare, one of the earliest and most distinctive flower displays of the gardening year. Its fall foliage color, orange to red-purple, is also considered among the best of the intermedia witch hazels, giving Diane strong two-season interest beyond the winter bloom. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Jelena Witch Hazel (Copper-Orange Winter Witch Hazel)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; witch hazel flower buds need real winter chill to open well, so bloom is most reliable in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 and can be sparse in mild winters.

directions: Jelena is widely regarded as one of the finest copper-orange witch hazel cultivars, its spidery, ribbon-petaled flowers opening a warm burnt-orange with a reddish flush toward the base of each petal, glowing against bare winter branches when little else in the garden shows any color. It carries some of the best fall foliage of any witch hazel cultivar as well, turning shades of orange, red, and yellow that echo the winter flower color, giving it real two-season value in a shaded border. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Golden Spirit Smokebush (Bright Chartreuse-Gold Smoke Tree)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Golden Spirit's gold foliage holds its brightest color in full sun but benefits from a little afternoon shade protection in the hottest part of zone 9 summer to avoid scorch.

directions: Golden Spirit is a smokebush selected for bright chartreuse-gold foliage that holds its color through the growing season before turning orange-red in fall, a striking contrast to the dark purple leaves of cultivars like Royal Purple and useful for lighting up a border planted with darker-foliaged companions. Airy, smoke-like plumes of tiny pinkish flowers appear in summer, giving the plant its common name, though the golden foliage itself is the main ornamental draw. Like other smokebush selections it is highly drought-tolerant once established and prefers lean, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter for a more compact, densely leaved shrub, which sacrifices that year's smoky flower plumes in exchange for larger, bolder foliage.

common_name: Double Take Orange Flowering Quince (Thornless Double-Flowered Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Double Take is bred to be thornless and essentially fruitless, so it can be handled and pruned without the scratches typical of older flowering quince cultivars.

directions: Double Take Orange carries fully double, ruffled, camellia-like flowers in bright orange, opening directly on the bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, and was specifically bred to be thornless, unlike the sharply spined branches of traditional flowering quince. Because the flowers are fully double and largely sterile, the shrub produces little to no fruit, putting its energy entirely into the showy bloom display rather than fruit set, and making it easier to handle for pruning, cutting for arrangements, or planting near a walkway. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next season's flower buds.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chardonnay Pearls' gold foliage holds its brightest color with a few hours of direct sun but benefits from afternoon shade in peak Gulf South summer heat to prevent scorch.

directions: Chardonnay Pearls is a slender deutzia selected for bright chartreuse-gold foliage that lights up a shaded border through the growing season, topped in mid-to-late spring by small, pearl-like white flower buds that open into star-shaped white blooms, giving the shrub a two-tone gold-and-white display. Its low, mounded, well-behaved habit fits foundation plantings and mixed borders where a compact flowering shrub with season-long foliage color is wanted, unlike plain-green deutzia cultivars that offer interest only during the spring bloom window. It tolerates partial shade better than many golden-leaved shrubs while still coloring and flowering well, and needs only light pruning right after bloom to keep a tidy, rounded shape.
